source: CARDI/MAFF Cashew Pest Management Guide (compiled from 3 sourced technical documents)
text:
Cashew crops in Cambodia face roughly 60 insect species, with 5 causing the most economic damage: tea mosquito bug, stem borer, mealybug, beetle/scarab grubs, and thrips.

Tea mosquito bug: the most economically damaging cashew pest. Adults suck sap from young shoots, flower clusters, seeds, and young fruit, leaving dark bruised marks. Most active feeding early morning (roughly 6-9am) and evening (roughly 4-8pm), especially July through December during and after the rainy season. Control: encourage natural predators, especially weaver ants; smoke/burn plant debris upwind during flowering season to drive pests away; use targeted insecticide spraying only when damage is observed rather than routine spraying, since broad-spectrum overuse harms natural predators and worsens infestations over time.

Stem borer: larvae bore into the trunk and roots, hidden inside the tree, present almost year-round. Signs: small holes with sap or wood-dust residue near the base of the trunk, yellowing leaves, dieback of small branches, and eventual tree death if severe. Control: insert flexible wire into the borer holes to kill larvae inside; seal exposed or damaged bark areas with a lime-based protective wash; apply used engine oil to the lower trunk (up to 1m from ground) during September-November and January to prevent egg-laying.

Mealybug: sucks sap from young leaves, shoots, and flowers, and secretes a waxy coating that makes control more difficult, especially once established on flowers and shoots.

Beetle/scarab grubs: damage shoots, flowers, and small twigs, most active at the start of the rainy season (roughly May-June).

Thrips: suck sap from leaves, shoots, and flowers, causing bronze or silvery discoloration; also act as a vector spreading viral disease between trees.

General principle across all these pests: routine field sanitation (removing and destroying damaged plant material), regular monthly inspection of shoots and branches, and targeted rather than blanket insecticide use are the consistently recommended first line of defense.
